title: Low‐Temperature Experimental Characterization of Magnetite‐Based Rock‐Bed Thermal Battery
abstract: ABSTRACT Rock bed thermal energy storage (RTES) systems are increasingly used as affordable and scalable solutions for low‐temperature heat storage. However, experimental investigations of magnetite packed beds under repeated charge–discharge cycles remain limited. This study experimentally evaluates the thermal performance of a horizontal cylindrical RTES system filled with magnetite and operated as a low‐temperature thermal battery for greenhouse applications. Two airflow strategies are compared over two successive cycles of charging and discharging: (i) unidirectional airflow during both charging and discharging (Model 1) and (ii) reversed airflow during discharge (Model 2). Thermal performance is analyzed through temperature stratification, heat transfer dynamics, energy recovery, and dimensionless performance indicators, including the Thermal Efficiency Index ( TEI ), Temperature Uniformity Index ( TUI ), Normalized Temperature Standard Deviation ( NTSD ), and Temperature Gradient Ratio ( TGR ). Results show that airflow reversal significantly enhances thermal propagation and heat extraction. Model 2 achieves a more pronounced thermal‐front response, generally higher TUI and TGR values, and higher energy recovery, delivering up to 30% more recovered heat during the first discharge period and approximately 15.79% more during the second discharge period compared with Model 1. Moreover, Model 2 exhibits higher TEI values across the investigated operating periods, with particularly noticeable advantages during the first discharge and second charging periods. These findings demonstrate that discharge flow reversal is an effective operating strategy for improving the responsiveness and heat‐recovery performance of low‐temperature magnetite RTES systems.
title_zh: Low‐Temperature Experimental Characterization of Magnetite‐Based Rock‐Bed Thermal Battery

title: Solar Photovoltaic Based Modular Electric Vehicle Battery Charging Using Interleaved Boost and Phase‐Shifted Full‐Bridge Converters
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper proposes direct charging of lithium‐ion batteries in electric vehicles (EVs) using standalone solar photovoltaic (PV) systems at distributed charging stations. A PV plant can be operated in an adaptive optimal mode to dynamically regulate its output power to match the aggregate charging power drawn by multiple lithium‐ion batteries, as reflected in the DC‐link voltage. To stabilize the DC‐link voltage and balance power between PV generation and battery load, a master–slave control strategy is used. In this setup, the DC‐link voltage controller acts as the master, generating a corrective duty cycle to reduce voltage changes. The MPPT (Maximum Power Point Tracking) controller, acting as the slave, provides the base duty cycle to extract the maximum power possible from the PV array. The resulting composite duty ratio drives a multiple‐phase interleaved boost DC–DC converter, improving power conversion efficiency and reducing input current ripple. A distributed phase‐shifted full‐bridge converter (PSFBC) is used to charge the batteries following the constant current–constant voltage (CC–CV) method. The proposed architecture is implemented using a modular three‐leg inverter, which is scalable and allows integration of higher‐rated PV arrays and additional battery charging channels without requiring any major modification in the control strategy, owing to the flexibility of the master–slave coordination mechanism. A multiple‐modular boost‐PSFB converter using four three‐phase inverter modules has been used for implementing the four‐phase IBC‐PSFB converter for 10.44 kW solar PV to charge four 72 V, 100 Ah Li‐ion batteries through MATLAB Simulink software. The control algorithm is also validated in real‐time using Typhoon‐HIL in virtual HIL mode for implementing a two‐phase IBC‐PSFB converter, based on a practical setup comprising a 2.2 kW solar PV system and two 72 V, 26 Ah Li‐ion batteries.
title_zh: Solar Photovoltaic Based Modular Electric Vehicle Battery Charging Using Interleaved Boost and Phase‐Shifted Full‐Bridge Converters

title: A novel unsupervised anomaly detection and traceability method for battery voltage inconsistency based on the time-segmented DBSCAN algorithm
abstract: Voltage inconsistencies in lithium-ion battery packs are a primary driver of performance degradation and thermal runaway. Accurate diagnosis from real-world operational data remains hindered by highly dynamic driving conditions, continuous measurement noise, and scarce labeled faults. To address these challenges, an unsupervised anomaly detection framework utilizing a time-segmented Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise algorithm is proposed. High-dimensional voltage features, capturing both transient fluctuations and long-term aging behaviors, are extracted via a multi-scale sliding window mechanism. Principal Component Analysis is subsequently applied to decouple absolute voltage levels from dynamic inconsistency patterns. Time-segmented clustering then facilitates highly efficient local anomaly detection, generating a continuous Consistency Health Index for the quantitative grading of individual cell health. The framework was rigorously validated using actual operational data from two distinct electric vehicles that experienced severe thermal runaway. The failed cells (Cell #126 in EV 1; Cells #52 and #53 in EV 2) were accurately flagged one full month prior to the catastrophic incidents, achieving significantly high Anomaly Signal-to-Noise Ratios of 8.98 and 10.18. Quantitative comparisons confirm the proposed methodology significantly outperforms benchmark algorithms in isolating true fault signals from background noise, fundamentally eliminating the ranking inversion issue across diverse battery systems.
title_zh: A novel unsupervised anomaly detection and traceability method for battery voltage inconsistency based on the time-segmented DBSCAN algorithm

title: Physics-constrained multi-task energy consumption prediction for the safe operation of embodied mobile robots
abstract: Reliable task-level energy assessment is essential for sustained mission execution and safe operation of battery-powered mobile robots under dynamic conditions. State of charge (SOC) and fixed-capacity estimates provide limited information about the effective energy reserve under changing electrical, thermal, and locomotion conditions. This study proposes a two-level indicator system comprising task-available energy (TAE) and a predictive relative risk margin. TAE characterizes the energy reserve available for a specific task under current operating conditions, extending conventional SOC-based assessment toward task-conditioned energy availability. An 85-day operational dataset covering five gait modes is segmented into task fragments. The proposed physics-constrained multi-task model combines categorical embeddings, stacked long short-term memory encoding, temporal attention, and current-state fusion to jointly predict TAE, future energy consumption, future minimum voltage, and future maximum battery temperature. On the independent test set, normalized root-mean-square error (NRMSE) values of 1.34%, 1.60%, 0.68%, and 0.59% are obtained for the four targets, respectively. Compared with the strongest energy-related baselines, the NRMSE values for TAE and future energy are reduced by 72.4% and 65.6%, respectively. The predictive relative risk margin integrates energy, voltage, and thermal constraints, achieving a coefficient of determination of 0.993, a risk-level agreement of 94.01%, and a dominant-risk-factor accuracy of 93.30%. This work reframes battery management as a task-aware predictive capability that integrates energy state assessment, operational risk evaluation, and autonomous decision-making, enabling safer and more reliable operation of mobile robots in dynamic environments.
title_zh: Physics-constrained multi-task energy consumption prediction for the safe operation of embodied mobile robots

title: Physics-inspired degradation modeling guided by dynamic orbits for battery health prognostics
abstract: Remaining useful life (RUL) prediction must be reliable for optimal operation, maintenance scheduling and lifecycle management of battery-powered systems. In practical applications, batteries are frequently subjected to fluctuating power demands and irregular operating schedules, resulting in condition-dependent capacity variations that can obscure the underlying slow degradation trend and challenge conventional RUL prediction methods. Building on the experimentally observed orbit-like degradation behavior under dynamic operating conditions, this study develops a physics-inspired degradation modeling framework, termed PhyOrbitNet, for battery RUL prediction. PhyOrbitNet jointly represents intra-cycle degradation manifestation and cross-cycle degradation propagation. In the feature learning stage, a mathematical framework is derived to describe the coupled evolution of fast-varying observables and slow-varying degradation variables in a high-dimensional phase space, and is reformulated as a cross-attention module within the Transformer architecture. Furthermore, considering the influence of historical degradation information, the dual form of a state-space model is derived and formulated as structured masked attention. A knowledge distillation mechanism is further introduced to transfer degradation representation capability to a student model driven solely by operating conditions, enabling long-term RUL prediction. Experimental results demonstrate that PhyOrbitNet provides accurate RUL prediction across different cells and lifetime stages under dynamic operating conditions.
title_zh: Physics-inspired degradation modeling guided by dynamic orbits for battery health prognostics

title: Integrated energy and thermal management for battery energy storage systems in range-extended electric vehicles based on generative adversarial imitation learning
abstract: Battery energy storage control and thermal regulation play a critical role in improving the energy efficiency and battery lifetime of range-extended electric vehicles (REEVs). However, the strong nonlinear coupling among battery power demand, thermal behavior, and range extender operation introduces a high-dimensional storage control problem, making it difficult to simultaneously achieve global optimality and real-time control. To address this challenge, a global optimization-guided generative adversarial imitation learning (GAIL)-based integrated energy and thermal management strategy is proposed to optimize battery storage operation and thermal regulation in REEVs. First, the coupling mechanism between energy management and thermal management is analyzed, and a multi-objective optimization framework is established to jointly minimize fuel consumption and battery aging cost. Offline dynamic programming (DP) is employed to generate globally optimal state–action trajectories, which serve as expert dataset for policy learning. Based on these expert data, a GAIL framework is developed to learn coordinated control policies for range extender power allocation and battery cooling demand through adversarial imitation learning. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed strategy achieves 97.82% of DP performance in weighted total cost while maintaining real-time feasibility. Compared with rule-based and reinforcement learning-based strategies, fuel consumption is reduced by 3.31%–10.65%, and battery aging cost decreases by 1.39%–1.67%. Furthermore, evaluation on an unseen real-world driving cycle provides preliminary evidence of the proposed strategy's adaptability and robustness.
title_zh: Integrated energy and thermal management for battery energy storage systems in range-extended electric vehicles based on generative adversarial imitation learning

title: Degradation-informed state-of-health estimation of lithium-ion batteries using a Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network
abstract: Lithium-ion batteries degrade during service through coupled electrochemical and thermal aging, causing capacity fade and increased operational risk. Accurate state-of-health (SOH) estimation is therefore required for battery health management. When only compact cycle-level descriptors are available, maintaining prediction accuracy together with model interpretability remains difficult. This study proposes a degradation-informed hyperparameter-optimized Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network (HPO-TabPFN) framework for SOH estimation. Each cycle is represented using temporal, energy-related and incremental-capacity descriptors, chronological context is constructed for TabPFN, and inference-related hyperparameters are optimized. Grid search, random search, particle swarm optimization and Bayesian optimization (BO) are evaluated under the same temporal validation protocol. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) is used to analyze local feature attribution, and Sobol analysis is used to quantify model-output sensitivity and interaction effects. On the evaluated NASA and CALCE cell sequences, hyperparameter optimization reduced the prediction error of TabPFN, and the Bayesian-optimized model achieved average mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) values of 0.2450% and 0.1800%, respectively. Under the same chronological delayed-label protocol, BO-TabPFN gave the lowest error among the unoptimized TabPFN and the evaluated baseline regressors on the tested cells. These results indicate that cycling-derived health indicators can support accurate tabular SOH estimation in the evaluated public datasets, while the NASA B05 case study illustrates how the fitted estimator depends on the selected health factors under the stated attribution and sensitivity settings.
title_zh: Degradation-informed state-of-health estimation of lithium-ion batteries using a Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network
